walkthroughs.body_html: In Republic Book VII, Plato imagines prisoners chained in a cave watching shadows cast by puppets behind them. One prisoner is freed, ascends past fire to the sun, and recognises true reality. The sun symbolises the Form of the Good. The allegory illustrates the ascent from doxa (opinion) through dianoia (mathematical reasoning) to noesis (intellectual vision).

In Physics II.3, Aristotle distinguishes four explanatory factors. The material cause is what something is made of (bronze for the statue); the formal cause is its shape or essence (the figure of Hermes); the efficient cause is what brings it about (the sculptor); the final cause is its purpose (to honour Hermes). For Aristotle, final causation is fundamental.

In Metaphysics Lambda (XII), Aristotle argues that the eternal motion of the heavens requires an eternal, immaterial, unmoving cause. This Prime Mover moves not by pushing but as a final cause: 'it moves as the beloved' (1072b3). The Prime Mover is pure actuality (actus purus), engaged in eternal self-thinking - 'thought thinking itself' (noesis noeseos).
